key_insight: Fine-tuned VLA models may still retain a lot of commonsense and world knowledge from their pretrained VLMs, but standard robotics benchmarks can hide this because failures may come from control, not memory. The paper’s key idea is to test knowledge by forcing the model to "answer through action" instead of language.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the ambiguity in evaluating embodied VLA models: when they fail on knowledge-sensitive tasks, it is unclear whether they forgot the knowledge or simply cannot execute the low-level action correctly. It introduces a way to separate knowledge retention from control/generalization issues.
method: Introduces Act2Answer, a lightweight protocol that converts VLM knowledge benchmarks into VLA evaluations.
Requires the agent to express its answer through an action, reducing reliance on text-only outputs.
Measures how much commonsense and factual knowledge survives after adapting VLMs to robotics tasks.
impact: This helps researchers diagnose whether VLA training preserves or erases pretrained knowledge, which is important for building embodied agents that are both capable and informed. Practitioners can use this evaluation style to compare models more fairly and identify whether failures are due to knowledge loss or control limitations.
visual_elements: Before/after pipeline showing VLM pretraining → VLA fine-tuning → Act2Answer evaluation.
Split-screen diagram contrasting "knowledge missing" vs "control failure".
Flowchart of how a benchmark question becomes an action-based response.
Simple score chart comparing retained knowledge across models or tasks.
paper_title: Does VLA Even Know the Basics? Measuring Commonsense and World Knowledge Retention in Vision-Language-Action Models
paper_authors: Nikita Kachaev, Andrey Moskalenko, Matvey Skripkin, Nikita Kurlaev, Daria Pugacheva
